topic.title: GPay is the word, UPI is the thing
topic.claim: When we say 'GPay kar do' for any UPI payment, one brand has won the one thing no ad can buy: becoming the word.
topic.behaviour: People say 'GPay kar do' whichever app they use. A Karan Johar story about a school snack counter that took 'only GPay' is the latest example.
topic.mechanism: The first app people learned becomes the name of the act. After that, rivals have to spend money on a habit that is already owned.
topic.group: Everyday UPI users who pay with PhonePe, Paytm or a bank app and still say 'GPay'
topic.moment: You're paying with PhonePe, but you tell the shopkeeper 'GPay kar diya'.

turn.believed: We pick the app that is best for us.
turn.actually: We pick the name that is already in our mouth, and the brand that owns the word owns the habit.

topic.villain: a market where the first brand to teach a habit gets the name of the habit for free
topic.because: Once a brand name becomes the verb, every payment by any app is free advertising for the first one. Rivals have to fight a word, not a product.

proof.fact: The article uses Karan Johar's school sports day anecdote, where the snack counter took only Google Pay, to show how 'GPay kar do' is said for any UPI payment, whichever app people use.

topic.payoff: Check your own habit: which app do you say out loud, and is it the one you actually use?
topic.send_to: The friend who still says 'GPay kar do' while paying with another app.
real_details: The anecdote came from Koffee with Karan season 9

topic.why_now: The anecdote went around this week and prompted a fresh look at how a brand name becomes a verb.

notes: The take's premise is wrong: Premise 1 is wrong: 'The app that taught most Indians UPI was Google Pay, and that is why its name became the word for UPI payment.' Google Pay (launched as Tez) was the top UPI app only for about 18 months, roughly 2019 to 2020. PhonePe led at points in 2018, passed Google Pay in October 2020, and has been the biggest UPI app since then. UPI handled about 2 billion transactions a month at that point. It now handles about 25 billion a month. So most Indians started using UPI while PhonePe was the leader, not Google Pay. Slide 7 also contradicts itself. It says 'the habit moved, and the word went with it,' but the habit moved from Google Pay to PhonePe and the word stayed 'GPay.' The other premises hold. Cashback is a fight over payments, not over the brand name. 'Xerox' is used as a generic verb in India. People do say 'GPay' for payments made on other apps. The 79% combined share is correct: it fell to 79% in May 2026, and in September 2026 it was PhonePe 45.6% plus Google Pay 32.2%.. How it actually works: Any UPI app sends a payment through NPCI's shared system. The shop's speaker only announces that money arrived, so which app you used never comes up at the counter. 'GPay' probably became the everyday word while Google Pay led in 2019–20, during UPI's first big growth among city users, and because it is short and easy to say. It stayed after PhonePe took the lead in October 2020 and grew much bigger. Of the two leaders, Google Pay has the smaller share (about 32%) but still owns the word. The everyday word follows whatever name caught on early and is easy to say, not which app people actually use most. Rebuild the post on the correct mechanism.

ledger.text: Mechanism: Google Pay caught on early and has a short, easy-to-say name. Once people adopt a brand name as the word for paying, it sticks even when they pay on another app. As a result, every UPI payment on any app gets called 'GPay', which gives Google Pay free, unpaid advertising. Rivals can win individual payments with cashback offers but cannot win the word.
ledger.sentence: Google Pay won the one thing no cashback can buy: every UPI payment, on any app, gets called GPay.

_ledger.text:
[cover] Google Pay won the one thing no ad can buy: [the word]
You say GPay even when another app moves the money.
 

[slide 1] You paid on PhonePe and said "GPay kar diya".
Google Pay got credit for a payment it never touched.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] The shopkeeper doesn't care which app you used. He just wants to see the money land.
Only you say a brand out loud.

[slide 3] Listen to how far the word travels:
– "GPay kar do" to the chaiwala with a Paytm QR
– "Maine GPay kar diya" in the flatmates group, from a bank app
– "GPay number bhejo" when you mean your UPI number

[slide 4] And it's not just the chai stall. On Koffee with Karan, Karan Johar told a story about his kids' school sports day.
The snack counter took "only GPay".

[slide 5] PhonePe and Google Pay together carry about 79% of UPI payments. Only part of that is GPay.
The word covers all of it. And every app outside it.

[slide 6] We like to think we pick the app that suits us best. Mostly we pick the name already in our mouth.

[slide 7] GPay caught on early and fits in one breath at a busy counter.
Once a word sticks, it stays put. Even when the money moves to another app.

[slide 8] So PhonePe and the rest are stuck in a weird fight. Every cashback offer can win them a payment.
None wins them the word. A PhonePe scratch card pays you, and you still say GPay out loud.

[slide 9] Nobody's being dumb here. GPay is just the shortest name in the queue.
But one brand gets said out loud all day, for free. The rest are paying for every single payment with offers.

[slide 10] Next time you're at a chai stall, catch which app comes out of your mouth.
Then look at which one is open on your phone.
If they don't match, you just ran an ad for Google Pay. Unpaid.

[end card] Come back to this the next time you hear yourself say "GPay kar diya".
Send to the friend who says "GPay kar do" while paying with PhonePe.

[caption] Google Pay won the one thing no cashback can buy: every UPI payment, on any app, gets called GPay.

"Bhaiya, GPay kar diya" after paying on PhonePe is a free ad for Google Pay, said out loud at the counter.

Send this to the friend who says "GPay kar do" with PhonePe already open on their phone.

[alt text] A ten-slide text post arguing that Google Pay has become the everyday word for any UPI payment in India. People say 'GPay kar do' while paying on PhonePe, Paytm or bank apps, while the shopkeeper only cares that the money arrived. It mentions Karan Johar's Koffee with Karan story about a school snack counter that took 'only GPay', and notes that PhonePe and Google Pay together carry about 79% of UPI payments, only part of which is GPay. It argues GPay caught on early and is easy to say, so the word stays even when people use other apps. Rivals can win payments with cashback offers but not the word. It ends by asking readers to catch which app they say out loud versus which one they actually use.

slides.why_swipe: How does a brand win a payment it didn't even process?

paragraphs: The shopkeeper doesn't care which app you used. He just wants to see the money land.
Only you say a brand out loud.
slides.why_swipe: Is this just one slip, or does everyone do it?

paragraphs:
Listen to how far the word travels:
– "GPay kar do" to the chaiwala with a Paytm QR
– "Maine GPay kar diya" in the flatmates group, from a bank app
– "GPay number bhejo" when you mean your UPI number
slides.why_swipe: If even famous people say it, how big is this?

paragraphs: And it's not just the chai stall. On Koffee with Karan, Karan Johar told a story about his kids' school sports day.
The snack counter took "only GPay".
slides.why_swipe: So how much of the market is actually GPay?

paragraphs: PhonePe and Google Pay together carry about 79% of UPI payments. Only part of that is GPay.
The word covers all of it. And every app outside it.
slides.why_swipe: Why does one name stick when the apps all work the same?

paragraphs: We like to think we pick the app that suits us best. Mostly we pick the name already in our mouth.
GPay caught on early and fits in one breath at a busy counter.
Once a word sticks, it stays put. Even when the money moves to another app.
slides.why_swipe: What does that mean for the brands fighting Google Pay?

paragraphs: So PhonePe and the rest are stuck in a weird fight. Every cashback offer can win them a payment.
None wins them the word. A PhonePe scratch card pays you, and you still say GPay out loud.
slides.why_swipe: So are we being played, or is this just how language works?

paragraphs: Nobody's being dumb here. GPay is just the shortest name in the queue.
But one brand gets said out loud all day, for free. The rest are paying for every single payment with offers.
slides.why_swipe: How do you check if you're doing it too?

paragraphs: Next time you're at a chai stall, catch which app comes out of your mouth.
Then look at which one is open on your phone.
If they don't match, you just ran an ad for Google Pay. Unpaid.

end.save: Come back to this the next time you hear yourself say "GPay kar diya".
end.send: Send to the friend who says "GPay kar do" while paying with PhonePe.
end.promise: How brands get inside Indian habits.

draft.alt_text: A ten-slide text post arguing that Google Pay has become the everyday word for any UPI payment in India. People say 'GPay kar do' while paying on PhonePe, Paytm or bank apps, while the shopkeeper only cares that the money arrived. It mentions Karan Johar's Koffee with Karan story about a school snack counter that took 'only GPay', and notes that PhonePe and Google Pay together carry about 79% of UPI payments, only part of which is GPay. It argues GPay caught on early and is easy to say, so the word stays even when people use other apps. Rivals can win payments with cashback offers but not the word. It ends by asking readers to catch which app they say out loud versus which one they actually use.
